svg.text: How /refactor turns standards findings into verified cleanup
Twelve steps, one batch at a time, every fix re-checked and re-gated before the next begins.

g.text: Point /refactor at the whole repo or one
folder, with an optional batch budget
Refuse to start without a config or without
git, and on uncommitted changes unless
Create a run ID and a repository lock so no
other lightsout run touches the same tree
Keeps the entire cleanup as one diff you can read,
Search source files for repeated names,
Detectors that read types need the repo’s
own TypeScript, and say so when it is
Leave out anything already accepted as known
debt, unless you asked for everything
Detection is deterministic code — no agent is ever
One batch is one kind of finding in one area
— a package, a top-level folder, or the repo
The most mechanical kinds run first, twelve
findings at most, and a finding spanning two
Freeze the list to disk and work from it —
Gives each agent a single coherent job instead of a
Run any code generator first, then lint,
type checks, tests, build, and coverage
Stop immediately if any gate is already
Skip this on a resumed run when an earlier
Proves any later failure was introduced by this run,
Check again immediately before each batch
If earlier batches already cleared these
findings, close the batch and spend no agent
Collect fresh size warnings for the batch’s
files — the frozen ones cite line numbers
Never pays an agent to fix something that is already
Batches run one at a time; the agent gets
the findings, the files they live in, and
Findings must be fixed or explained; size
warnings are judged against your documented
It may run only the commands your config
allows, works under a time limit, and
Changes structure only — the behavior has to survive
Re-run the gates, scoped to the packages
that changed, with coverage always on
Try up to two lightweight repairs when a
Send a coverage-only failure to a
test-writing agent; a mixed failure goes
back to the refactor agent first
Stops a batch that broke the build from reaching the
When the quick repairs run out, a read-only
It either grants one guided retry or rules
If the gates are still red after that, the
run stops with the diagnosis attached as
Buys judgment exactly once, instead of retrying
Check again — the code rules, and a copied
block that merely moved is not gone
Gone counts as resolved; still there with
nothing changed counts as declined, with the
Partly fixed earns one more pass, and
whatever survives that is recorded as
Work finished without a report still counts, and
changed files come from git, minus generated output
Three declines in a row end the run — the
pattern is systemic, and more spend will not
A refusal on scope grounds counts as a
decline and the run carries on
A harness rate limit or your batch budget
parks the run instead of failing it
Each batch is saved before the next begins, and
declines are read back — resuming re-runs nothing
Check the whole scope once more and report
findings before and after, one line per kind
A parked run reports no burn-down — resume
Keep every batch outcome, retry, token cost,
and point of friction in one folder
Turns the cleanup into a number you can check rather
Read each declined batch alongside the

Fix it by hand, or accept it as known debt
Review the working-tree diff and commit it —
Leaves the last call on unfixed debt with a human

svg.text: The engine never commits. It hands back a measured before-and-after and a diff you review.
